bullets: Un sistema rápido cruza el lunes con humedad y dinámica limitadas: solo chubascos ligeros y acumulaciones mínimas en terreno alto.
Una cresta de alta presión trae tiempo seco desde el martes hasta al menos media semana.
Para Thanksgiving y el fin de semana sigue posible un patrón más activo, pero los ensambles no coinciden (confianza baja).

sections.Key Messages:
- Mild and dry conditions expected through Thanksgiving.
- Snow is expected late Friday and through Saturday, primarily
  over the Park Range. The Flat Tops and central Colorado
  mountains are also expected to be impacted.
- An unsettled pattern looks to continue into next week with
  potential for more mountain snow, but details remain
  uncertain.
sections.Discussion:
Issued at 944 PM MST Wed Nov 25 2026
MILD AND DRY CONDITIONS THROUGH THANKSGIVING:
A ridge is situated overhead with little more than high clouds
passing through the region. Thanksgiving Day will be
characterized by near-normal moisture, and as a result, region-
wide weather will be calm. Temperatures will be 5 to 10 degrees
above normal Thanksgiving Day as well.
SNOWY AFTER THANKSGIVING INTO THE WEEKEND:
On Friday, moisture originating from a PacNW AR will descend
into the Intermountain West through northwesterly flow. The bulk
of that moisture will reside to our north, but ensembles are
indicating that the northeastern corner of our CWA will get
clipped by PWAT's up to 200% of normal. This sparks our next
round of impactful weather. The onset of measurable
precipitation is expected to occur late afternoon to early
evening Friday with most precipitation driven by orographics and
anchored to the high terrain. Though moisture is expected to
begin declining around sunrise Saturday, models are showing the
strongest snow rates during this period. This is mostly driven
by a transient shortwave embedded in the northwesterly flow, and
as such, we should see an uptick in snow rates both over the
mountains and into some higher elevation valleys and basins in
north-central Colorado through the late morning and into the
afternoon.
As seen in the latest forecast, snow totals are on the rise.
With the upward trend of snow totals for the weekend storm, the
low end snow scenario looks safely at or above advisory level
(6+ inches) for the Park Range. The NBM backs this up with a
greater than 80% probability of 6 or more inches of snow above
9000 feet, which would include Rabbit Ears Pass. Below this
elevation though, probability of advisory-level snow
accumulations sharply drop off. For those areas in the Park
Range expected to receive the bulk of snowfall, the question is
what the high end scenario could be. Per the NBM, probabilities
of accumulations exceeding a foot stand at over 70%. In spite of
the high chances, we are cautious to call for 12+ inches over
the Park Range just yet due to lacking consistency between
forecasts. Though guidance is trending towards higher
accumulations, we will wait to see where model guidance settles
before speculating on amounts.
Though impacts look greatest for the Park Range, concerns for
impactful snowfall over the Flat Tops and central Colorado
mountains are manifesting as well. The former is looking more
and more favorable to hit advisory-level snow. Confidence has
decreased on exact values over the past twelve hours, but this
is due to 75th percentile snow forecasts jumping up. So, just
like the Park Range, forecasts are trending upwards for snow
totals in the Flat Tops. As for the latter, confidence in
accumulations has notably increased according to the NBM, though
it is still anticipated to see the least precipitation among
the areas of interest. Given the northerly track of the storm,
elevations at pass level and below are likely to struggle to
reach 6 inches. However, with roads likely to be busier with
post-holiday travel, even lighter accumulations will pose
heightened travel risks. As such, be mindful of difficult
driving conditions through the mountains should you find
yourself on the roads Saturday.
